title: Comments of Tyonek Tribal Conservation District opposing the proposed preliminary permit for the DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea-Compute and Infrastructure Hub Project under P-15423.

documents.name: TTCD-Comments_P-15423-000_DeepGreen.pdf
documents.text:
November 2, 2026

Submitted via FERC’s eFiling system

Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
12225 Wilkins Avenue
Rockville, Maryland 20852


Re: DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC Notice of Preliminary Permit Application (P-15423-000);
Comments of Tyonek Tribal Conservation District

Dear Secretary Reese and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission:

Tyonek Tribal Conservation District (TTCD) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Federal
Energy Regulatory Commission’s (FERC) Notice of Preliminary Permit Application for the proposed
DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub Project (DeepGreen project; P-15423-
000) located in Alaska’s East Foreland region of Upper Cook Inlet. We are writing to request that
FERC deny the preliminary permit application as currently proposed. The proposed project is
unprecedented both in scale and with the inclusion of subsea-compute hives (data center pods).
This letter also addresses environmental concerns that should be investigated, if permitted.

Current Hydrokinetic Landscape

At this time, there are only three hydrokinetic projects licensed by FERC in the United States. Two of
these projects are hydrokinetic testing facilities, where companies can test their designs. These
projects are located in the marine environment off the coast of Maine and Oregon and are
authorized to produce 0.05 megawatts (MW) and 20 MW, respectively. The other project is located
in Alaska; it is actively generating power for the Village of Igiugig via two hydrokinetic turbines
anchored into the Kvichak River. This project is authorized to produce 0.07 MW.

There are currently 11 active hydrokinetic preliminary permits in the United States, two of which
are located in Alaska. The Alaska projects being investigated are also located in the East Forelands
of Upper Cook Inlet. Their preliminary permits authorize a capacity of 5 MW and 2 MW. There have
been several other hydrokinetic projects investigated in the Cook Inlet, and as of yet no company
has found the environment of Cook Inlet to be a feasible location for producing hydrokinetic power.
The draw to Cook Inlet, particularly the East Forelands, is the strong tidal currents occurring in this
area. However, the shortfalls are many, including a silty substrate making anchoring extremely
dif�icult, a silt-laden water column that is extremely abrasive, and a critically important marine
environment that supports valuable sport, commercial, and subsistence �isheries, as well as the
endangered Cook Inlet beluga whale.

The scale of the DeepGreen project, which includes 330-350 marine hydrokinetic turbines
producing 100 MW, is an extreme anomaly to what is currently licensed in the U.S. and what is
 currently being investigated in Alaska. This proposed design is impractical in size, particularly at
this narrow location of Cook Inlet. Past and current studies in the East Forelands have not found a
way to deploy one marine hydrokinetic turbine in this environment, much less over 300 turbines. If
FERC decides to license this project, it should only be if the proposal is scaled down considerably to
study the potentiality of deploying one hydrokinetic turbine in Cook Inlet.

Utilizing marine energy to power data center pods is both a novel and speculative concept. Nowhere
in the world does this exist. The proposal to deploy 66 data center pods in Cook Inlet is an
ostentatious concept that has no precedence. The marine environment of Cook Inlet is particularly
sensitive and already experiences multiple pressures that stress and harm the �ish and wildlife.
Each new additional source of disturbance adds to existing pressures that can compound impacts
across the ecosystem. TTCD believes that deploying data center pods into the already stressed
marine environment of Cook Inlet adds unacceptable risks to our �ish, wildlife, and livelihoods.

The Environment of Cook Inlet

Cook Inlet is an ecologically signi�icant and environmentally sensitive marine ecosystem, supporting
productive commercial, recreational, and subsistence �isheries, diverse marine and coastal wildlife,
and communities whose cultures and livelihoods are deeply connected to its natural resources. The
Cook Inlet region is home to the majority of Alaska’s population, making the health of the Inlet
especially important to the state’s communities, economy, and public resources. Its salmon, halibut,
and other �ish populations depend on the health and connectivity of the inlet’s estuarine,
freshwater, and nearshore habitats. Cook Inlet is also home to the endangered Cook Inlet beluga
whale, a genetically distinct population that faces ongoing challenges from habitat disturbance,
underwater noise, pollution, and other human activities. At the same time, the Inlet serves as a
major transportation corridor for cargo vessels, tankers, �ishing �leets, and other marine traf�ic,
creating potential risks from vessel strikes, underwater noise, fuel or oil spills, and disturbances to
sensitive wildlife and habitats. The combination of ecological importance, population density,
subsistence use, commercial activity, and increasing development pressures makes careful
stewardship of Cook Inlet essential to protecting its �isheries, wildlife, communities, and long-term
ecological health.

The proposed DeepGreen project raises signi�icant concerns about impacts to Cook Inlet’s
endangered beluga whales and sensitive marine habitat. Belugas rely on sound to communicate,
navigate, locate prey, and avoid threats, making underwater noise a critical concern for the recovery
of this endangered population. The proposed facility’s noise could interfere with these essential
behaviors and potentially disrupt the seasonal movements of belugas through the East Forelands,
an important passage between feeding and calving areas. Because this narrow corridor is also
ecologically important for �ish migration, the cumulative effects of installing 66 data center pods
and more than 300 turbine generators warrant careful scrutiny before the project proceeds.

The project also raises substantial concerns about the long-term health of Cook Inlet �isheries,
which sustain Alaska Native subsistence practices, commercial �ishing livelihoods, local
communities and �isheries, and the cultural identity of Alaskans. Adult salmon returning to streams
north of Nikiski must pass through this corridor, and setnet �ishing sites are located within three



                                                  2
 miles of the proposed facility. Juvenile salmon use Cook Inlet as a critical migration corridor, feeding
area, and transitional habitat as they move from freshwater streams and rivers toward the ocean.

Potential risks of the proposed project include copper releases, elevated water temperatures, and
the discharge of nearly 100 megawatts of waste heat into the marine environment. The applicant
has not identi�ied the mechanism it would use to manage this heat discharge, leaving important
questions about thermal impacts on �ish and wildlife and the broader aquatic ecosystem
unanswered. Further clari�ication is also needed regarding cooling-system chemicals, including
whether PFAS or other persistent contaminants could enter Cook Inlet. Given the ecological
importance of this region and the uncertainty surrounding the project’s potential impacts, a
rigorous assessment of noise, water quality, thermal pollution, �isheries, and cumulative effects is
essential to protecting Cook Inlet’s natural resources and the communities that depend on them.

Conclusion

While TTCD is hopeful that a feasible and unharmful marine energy project can be developed in
Alaska, we believe that this is the wrong project in the wrong place. Cook Inlet is a uniquely
sensitive marine environment that supports endangered Cook Inlet beluga whales, juvenile and
returning salmon, generational �isheries, and communities that depend on these resources for their
livelihoods, subsistence, and cultural identity. The proposed site lies within an already busy and
economically important corridor where marine transportation, �ishing activity, coastal
communities, and wildlife all compete for space and rely on a healthy, functioning ecosystem.
Introducing an unprecedented, speculative, and oversized industrial facility, with more than 300
hydrokinetic turbines, 66 data center pods, and 100 MW of waste heat, into this narrow and
ecologically signi�icant passage presents substantial risks. The protection of Cook Inlet’s marine
ecosystem and the resources it sustains must take precedence over advancing a project of this scale
without compelling evidence that it is a practicable design in the �irst place.

Sincerely,




Laurie Stuart, EdD | Executive Director
